Triggers.value: Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs

vignette: Three years ago, during a high-risk warrant service in a sprawling walk-up, Adrian Vance’s life fractured. He moved through the stairwell in complete darkness when the front door kicked in. A sedan with a dented quarter panel and a rusted rim screamed past the building, fishtailing into a densely packed block party where hundreds of people jostled in the narrow streets. Inside the target apartment, the exchange was chaotic. Uniformed backup flooded the hallway, tactical gear clinking, rifle magazines glinting. Adrian took cover behind a doorway, cordite and wet concrete burning his throat, his heart hammering as he waited for the all-clear. He survived, but the night burned itself into his nervous system. In the months that followed, Adrian had come to believe the world remained a place where silence instantly turns to violence. When he woke at two to the heavy dark of his bedroom, the absence of light tightened his chest, and the urge to pour a drink or swallow pills became automatic. The same pattern took hold the moment he spotted a car with a slightly bent fender in the studio lot, or when clients filled the glass conference room, their overlapping voices and close quarters making his breath shallow. In those moments, he would press his palms over his face, slip out the service exit, and deliberately reroute his commute away from the precinct, ensuring he never saw police patches or glinting gear. The dark, the vehicles, the crowds—each reliably drove him toward the bottle and the retreat. He drank to quiet phantom sirens, hid his eyes to escape imagined flashlights, and avoided duty talk to keep old panic at bay. The habits that formed out of survival slowly calcified into a wall between him and his former life. As a graphic designer, Adrian used to thrive on collaborative sessions in downtown studios, but now he would take late shifts to avoid rush-hour traffic that resembled the chase. When clients gathered around his drafting table, pressing close to review layouts, his shoulders would lock, and he would suddenly need to step out to check the server room, his hands trembling against the cool metal doorframe. At home, the distance grew heavier. His ex-wife stopped asking where he was when the nights grew quiet, and eventually stopped waiting altogether. The avoidance that once kept him safe had quietly hollowed out his marriage, leaving him navigating a life of measured exits and empty bottles. Now, at thirty-three, the cycle has tightened beyond his control. He scans every parked car on his route to the studio, counts the steps between his desk and the exit, and wakes repeatedly with his sheets tangled around his ankles. The more he drinks to numb the anticipation, the more his body bristles at ordinary sounds; the more he turns his face away, the more the dark feels like a threat waiting to materialize. He finally walked into the clinic because the quiet of his apartment has become unbearable, and he is terrified that one more night will push him past the point of return. What he hopes for is simply to stop running from the present, to sit in a room without his hands over his face, and to believe that the night is just the night.
